topics.title: Intro to Alg Confusion
topics.text:
Hello, I'm back with more confusion. I don't wanna seem spammy but I also wanna make sure I understand my mistakes. Problem 20.54: The graphs of $y=-|x-a|+b$ and $y=|x-c|+d$ intersect at the points $(2,5)$ and $(8,3)$. Find $a+c$.

My solution (which is not correct; I'm not sure why, so can someone please explain?): Since we know two intersection points of the two graphs, we can make 4 equations: $5=-|2-a|+b, 5=|2-c|+d, 8=-|3-a|+b,$ and $8=|3-c|+d$. We know the first two are equal, and doing some rearranging gives $|2-c|+|2-a|=b-d$. We can do the same for the last two equations and find that $|3-c|+|3-a|=b-d=|2-c|+|2-a|$. From here you can do some casework, and you will come to the case where both $a$ and $c$ are less than or equal to $3$ but greater than $2$, making $3-c$ and $3-a$ nonnegative but also making $2-a$ and $2-c$ negative. From here we have $3-c+3-a=-2+c-2+a \implies 6-(a+c)=-4+(a+c) \implies 2(a+c)=10 \implies a+c=5.$ I get the book solution which gives $a+c$ to be 10; why is mine wrong? Thanks.
